items.finding: The claim's opening frame says the comparison was salt water given to the same people on another day; that is not this study, which had a drug-free baseline scan and no placebo infusion, in an open design.
items.reason: The claim's own Vollenweider sentence already said 'In an open study without a dummy condition', and its comparator field already named the drug-free baseline, so the fault was only in the opening frame, which spoke for all five sources. The frame now says 'in every study read here but one open study, where the comparison was the same people's drug-free baseline', and the plain line says the same in plain words.
items.evidence: Vollenweider et al. (1997b), p. 10, Experimental procedures 2.2 (second reader's blind anchor); claim field statement, 1st sentence, and plain

items.finding: This source gives no support to 'the changes pass within minutes to a couple of hours of the end of the infusion': nothing in it measures symptoms after the infusion stopped.
items.reason: Accepted, and tightened further on my own reading. Only two of the five sources rated symptoms again after the infusion stopped. Krystal et al. (1994) state on the rendered pp. 203 and 205 that positive symptom scores and perceptual alteration scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end; Malhotra's last rating, at 90 minutes (30 minutes after the end of the 1-hour infusion), is 21.5 against 18.7 and is not marked as differing from the salt-water day (Table 1, rendered p. 304). Nothing read here supports an upper bound of two hours, so the sentence now reads 'where symptoms were rated again after the infusion stopped, they had gone or nearly gone within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour of its end', and the plain line matches.
items.evidence: Krystal et al. (1994), p. 203, Results > Positive Symptoms, 1st paragraph, and p. 205, Perceptual Aberration; Malhotra et al. (1996), Table 1, p. 304

items.finding: The CADSS statistic in the magnitude (F6,96 = 46.0, n = 17) is from the text; Figure 2's legend says n = 18, and the degrees of freedom fit 17, so the text is right.
items.reason: The claim and anchor 5 already use the text's n = 17. Checked on the rendered p. 205: dose F2,32 = 65.0 and dose x time F6,96 = 46.0 both fit 17 people, and the card's reporting issue 0 records the discrepancy. No change needed.
items.evidence: Krystal et al. (1994), p. 205, Results > Perceptual Alterations > CADSS; claim evidence[5]

items.finding: 'Distortions of real stimuli rather than hallucinations' is a fair paraphrase, but the same page reports ideas of reference with paranoid content and formal thought disorder at the larger amount, so the sentence should not be read as saying that nothing psychosis-like occurred.
items.reason: Confirmed on the rendered pp. 203 and 209: the Results say hallucinatory behaviour was limited to illusory experiences in all sensory domains, and the Comment says ketamine elicited paranoia, loose associations, ideas of reference and unusual thought content. The clause is already in anchor 6's extracted text, so no new anchor was needed; the statement now carries it beside the illusions sentence, and the plain line adds that people became suspicious and their thinking became muddled.
items.evidence: Krystal et al. (1994), pp. 203 and 209; claim evidence[6]

items.finding: Two editorial inferences in the Malhotra sentence are not printed in the paper: the 'SD' label on the item values and the 'floor of 3'.
items.reason: Confirmed on the rendered pp. 303-304: the item means print as a mean and a plus-or-minus figure with no label, while Table 1's footnote b labels the table values mean and SEM. The claim no longer prints an SD label on the item values; the magnitude says instead that the paper does not say which it is. The floor of 3 is kept but its basis is now stated in the claim ('each a three-item score whose floor is 3').
items.evidence: Malhotra et al. (1996), p. 303 (item means) and p. 304, Table 1 footnote b

items.finding: The claim's duration wording is only partly shown by this source: the BPRS was last rated at +90 minutes, when the total was 21.5 against 18.7 and not flagged as significant; later ratings were not made. The unchanged hostility-suspiciousness factor (F = 0.1, p = .90; 1 of 15 rose) bears on any statement that ketamine produced paranoid symptoms in this sample and was not in the claim.
items.reason: Both confirmed on the rendered Table 1 (p. 304) and p. 303: only the +55 values carry the p < .001 mark, and the Results say the hostility-suspiciousness analysis of variance revealed no significant effects. Both are now in the statement, and the hostility result in the magnitude; anchor 7 already carries the F = 0.1, p = .90 value.
items.evidence: Malhotra et al. (1996), Table 1 and Results, pp. 303-304; claim evidence[7]

items.finding: The BPRS analyses print error degrees of freedom of 81 to 82, impossible for 15 people tested twice at three time points, so the BPRS p values are likely too small.
items.reason: The claim cites only the Malhotra means and the item-level t test, never a BPRS analysis-of-variance p value, so nothing in it rests on those degrees of freedom. The card records the problem as reporting issue 1 and the second reader confirmed it independently. No change needed.
items.evidence: Malhotra et al. (1996), pp. 303-304; card sc_malhotra_1996 reporting_issues[1]

items.finding: Two qualifiers a reader needs: the BPRS hallucinatory-behavior item was deliberately scored so that perceptual distortions as well as hallucinations counted, and the authors detected no formal thought disorder or language disorganisation apart from modest alogia changes.
items.reason: Both read on the rendered pages: p. 109 (continuing from p. 108) states that the original, wider item description was used so that both perceptual distortions and hallucinations could be scored for that item, and p. 114 states that the study did not detect formal thought disorder or language disorganisation during the conditions tested, with the exception of modest effects on the alogia subscale. No existing anchor carried either, so a new anchor was added (evidence_add, pp. 108-109 and 114). It enters as ai-located and will need a second reader's check; the claim is at draft already, so no ladder status changed.
items.evidence: Newcomer et al. (1999), pp. 108-109, Methods > Clinical Assessments; p. 114, Discussion, 2nd paragraph

items.finding: 'In 15 men held at measured steady blood levels' overstates what Newcomer measured: blood was sampled at 0, 20, 60 and 120 minutes, steady state by 30 minutes is the authors' calculation, and the smallest condition never rose above the assay threshold.
items.reason: Same wording as in cl_ket_acute_memory_attention, where the second reader raised it. The phrase is now 'given three fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels', which matches the claim's own exposure field and needs no number not already anchored.
items.evidence: Newcomer et al. (1999), p. 113, Results > Plasma Results and Figure 6; claim field statement

items.finding: '13 of 15 people recalled less and 9 of 15 scored lower on the attention measure' names no comparison: the paper's counts are falls from each person's own pre-infusion level at 55 minutes on the ketamine day, not ketamine-minus-salt-water differences, and the salt-water means also dipped at 10 and 55 minutes.
items.reason: Read word for word on the rendered p. 303: nine of 15 showed decreases in attention from baseline at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion, thirteen of 15 decreases in free recall and nine of 14 in recognition. The statement, the magnitude and anchor 0's extracted text now say so, the recognition count is added for completeness, and the plain line carries the point, because a reader would otherwise take the counts for a responder rate against the salt-water day. Anchor 0 keeps its ai-checked status: the correction is the checking reader's own finding, made at the stated place.

items.finding: 'Recover within about an hour or two of the end of the infusion' rests on post hoc tests that were no longer significant, not on a demonstrated return; and Newcomer gives it no support at all, because cognition was tested only during the steady-state infusion.
items.reason: Accepted, with the count corrected: two of the three studies did test after the infusion stopped (Malhotra at 90 and 120 minutes, that is 30 and 60 minutes after the end; Krystal at the 80-minute rating, 40 minutes after the end of a 40-minute infusion), while Newcomer tested only during the infusion. The sentence now reads 'in the two studies that tested again after the infusion had stopped, were no longer detectably lower within about an hour of its end', the limits sentence says one of the three never tested anyone afterwards, and the plain line matches.
items.evidence: Malhotra et al. (1996), p. 303 and Figure 1 legend; Krystal et al. (1994), p. 207 and Figure 4; Newcomer et al. (1999), p. 112 and card sc_newcomer_1999 outcomes.operationalization

for_senior_author: sc_newcomer_1999, interpretation gap: the card rates it minor, the second reader would rate it moderate, because the abstract's headline (memory affected at or below the concentrations producing other symptoms, memory impairment first and other symptoms after) rests on one paired comparison that is one-tailed without saying so, at a concentration that was below the assay limit and never measured. The card's own 'claimed' text documents all of this; only the label is in question, and the brief keeps interpretation-gap differences out of the card.

Risk-of-bias domains, three cards: on sc_krystal_1994 and sc_malhotra_1996 the second reader notes that RoB 2's signalling questions would more usually give 'some concerns' rather than 'high' for probable unblinding without documented deviations; on sc_newcomer_1999 it notes that 'some concerns' would be defensible for the objective memory tasks, so a claim resting on paragraph recall alone is less affected. None of these changes an overall judgment and none was written into a card. The last one bears on the risk-of-bias downgrade of cl_ket_acute_memory_attention, which is currently minus 1 for all its outcomes together.

sc_krystal_1994: the second reader suggests a per-outcome note in the domain table saying that the card-sorting analysis is a between-person comparison outside the within-person design. The card says this in key finding 10 and reporting issue 7; whether the domain table should repeat it is an editorial choice.
